questions.stem: Five minutes after IV iodinated contrast is given for a CT scan, a client reports itching and a tight throat. The nurse sees hives on the chest and hears wheezing. Blood pressure has dropped from 132/80 to 84/50 mm Hg, and heart rate is 124/min. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Stop the contrast and give IM epinephrine as prescribed
Call for help and give oxygen and IV fluids
Give oral diphenhydramine and watch for 30 minutes
Finish the scan quickly before treating the reaction
Sit the client upright with the legs hanging down

rationale.correct: Contrast anaphylaxis: stop the contrast, give IM epinephrine, support airway and circulation and document the reaction for future premedication or alternatives.

perOption.c1: Hives, wheezing, throat tightness and hypotension minutes after contrast show a severe reaction.
perOption.c2: Kidney injury develops over 24 to 72 hours, not minutes.
perOption.c3: Vasovagal reactions cause a slow heart rate without hives or wheezing.
perOption.c4: Panic does not cause hives and hypotension.
perOption.a3: Antihistamines alone do not treat anaphylaxis.
perOption.a4: The reaction must be treated at once.
perOption.a5: Hypotension is treated with the client lying with the legs raised unless breathing needs otherwise.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

perOption.r3: Rapid breathing and new confusion are sepsis warning signs.
perOption.r5: Falling blood pressure and low urine output suggest worsening sepsis.

questions.stem: The nurse is collecting a sputum specimen for culture. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Plan the collection for early morning, before breakfast
Label the specimen and send it to the lab promptly
Have the client rinse the mouth with water
Have the client take deep breaths and cough deeply into a sterile container

perOption.c: Brings up sputum from the lungs.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is scheduled for a cardiac catheterization in the morning. Which actions should the nurse take before the procedure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask about earlier reactions to contrast dye
Check the serum creatinine
Ask the provider about holding metformin around the procedure
Mark and record the pedal pulses
Give a large high-fat breakfast to prevent hypoglycemia
Apply a heating pad to the groin to dilate the artery

rationale.correct: Before catheterization: contrast allergy history, creatinine, metformin plan, NPO status, consent and baseline pulses.

perOption.c: Metformin is held in at-risk clients to prevent lactic acidosis.
perOption.d: A baseline helps detect circulation problems afterward.
perOption.e: The client is usually NPO before the procedure.
perOption.f: This is not part of preparation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's telemetry shows a new irregularly irregular rhythm at 132/min with no clear P waves. The client feels palpitations but is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 mm Hg. Which risk should the nurse keep in mind when planning care?

options.text: Rapid progression to complete heart block
Stroke from a clot that forms in the atria
Hypoglycemia from a rapid heart rate
Pneumonia from reduced lung expansion during the fast rhythm

rationale.correct: New atrial fibrillation raises stroke risk; rate control, anticoagulation assessment and monitoring for symptoms are key.

perOption.a: Atrial fibrillation does not usually lead to heart block.
perOption.b: Atrial fibrillation lets blood pool in the atria and form clots that can travel to the brain.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the stroke risk of atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: On the first day after a hysterectomy, a client's urine output has been 20 mL/hr for 2 hours through an indwelling catheter. Heart rate is 96/min and blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the IV fluid rate to 250 mL/hr
Look for a kinked or blocked catheter, then assess fluid status
Give a dose of IV furosemide to increase the client's urine output
Document the output and recheck it at the end of the shift

rationale.correct: Low urine output after surgery: check the catheter first, then assess volume status and report; never give diuretics without assessing for hypovolemia.

perOption.a: The nurse needs a prescription and should first check the cause.
perOption.b: A blocked catheter is a quick, fixable cause; then the nurse assesses for hypovolemia and reports.
perOption.c: Diuretics can worsen hypovolemia and need a prescription.
perOption.d: Low output for 2 hours needs action now.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin for a mechanical heart valve (target INR 2.5 to 3.5) has these results: INR 4.6 and platelets 48,000/mm3. Complete the sentences.

content.template: The INR is {{b1}} the client's target range. The platelet count means the nurse should {{b2}}.

options.text: above
within
below
use bleeding precautions, such as a soft toothbrush and no IM injections
encourage contact sports to raise the platelets
give aspirin to prevent clots

rationale.correct: High INR and low platelets both raise bleeding risk; report them and use bleeding precautions.

perOption.b2:b: Activity does not raise platelets and raises injury risk.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client comes to the emergency department after watching a movie in a dark theater. The client has sudden severe pain in the right eye, blurred vision with halos around lights, a headache, nausea and vomiting. The right eye is red, and the pupil is mid-dilated and does not react to light. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Notify the provider and prepare drugs to lower eye pressure
Give the prescribed antiemetic and analgesic
Dilate the pupil further with prescribed drops to help the eye drain
Patch the eye and send the client home to rest in a dark room
Give an oral decongestant for the headache and stuffy nose

parameters.text: Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency: lower eye pressure quickly with drops and systemic drugs, avoid dilating drugs and prepare for laser treatment.

perOption.c1: Sudden eye pain, halos, a red eye, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and vomiting after time in the dark point to angle-closure glaucoma.
perOption.c2: Migraine does not cause a red eye with a fixed pupil.
perOption.c3: Conjunctivitis does not cause severe pain and a fixed pupil.
perOption.c4: Detachment causes painless flashes and a curtain over vision.
perOption.a1: This is an emergency that can cause blindness within hours.
perOption.a2: Treating nausea and pain lowers pressure from vomiting and eases distress.
perOption.a5: Some decongestants can worsen angle closure.
perOption.p2: Directly show the response to treatment.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize acute angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.stem: A client has burns of different depths after a kitchen fire. For each area, indicate the burn depth.

rows.text: Red, dry, painful skin on the forearm that blanches, with no blisters
Moist, pink skin with large blisters on the hand that is very painful
Pale, mottled skin on the chest with reduced sensation and slow capillary refill
White, leathery, dry skin on the leg with no pain when touched

rationale.correct: Burn depth: superficial (red, no blisters), superficial partial (moist, blistered, painful), deep partial (pale, less sensation), full-thickness (leathery, insensate).

perOption.r2:c2: Moist, blistered and very painful is superficial partial-thickness.
perOption.r2:c3: Deep partial burns are paler and less moist.
perOption.r3:c3: Pale, mottled skin with reduced sensation is deep partial-thickness.
perOption.r3:c4: Full-thickness burns are leathery and insensate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Classify burn depth.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old client arrives at the emergency department with chest pressure that started 30 minutes ago and spreads to the left arm. The client is sweating and anxious. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Draw a troponin level and wait for the result before doing anything else
Get a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of the client's arrival
Give a large glass of water and have the client lie flat
Send the client for a chest x-ray to look for pneumonia

rationale.correct: Suspected acute coronary syndrome: 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, aspirin unless contraindicated, oxygen if hypoxemic, and rapid reperfusion for STEMI.

perOption.a: Troponin may be normal early; the ECG is needed first.
perOption.b: A rapid ECG identifies STEMI, which needs emergency reperfusion.
perOption.c: This does not treat or diagnose the problem.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A 9-month-old who attends day care has had vomiting and watery diarrhea for 2 days and has refused the bottle since this morning. Which group of findings indicates severe dehydration?

options.text: Moist mouth, tears present and a soft, flat, normal fontanelle
Sunken fontanelle, no tears, lethargy and slow refill
Slightly dry mouth and fewer wet diapers than usual
Normal heart rate, alert and drinking eagerly

rationale.correct: Severe dehydration in infants: lethargy, sunken fontanelle and eyes, no tears, very dry mouth, cool mottled skin and delayed capillary refill.

perOption.a: These suggest little or no dehydration.
perOption.b: These show severe dehydration with poor perfusion.
perOption.d: These suggest mild or no dehydration.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with stable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse is receiving an IV amiodarone infusion. Which finding should the nurse report right away?

options.text: Heart rate has slowed from 168/min to 92/min in sinus rhythm
Blood pressure has fallen to 78/44 mm Hg with lightheadedness
The client reports a metallic taste in the mouth
The IV site is slightly red along the vein without any swelling

rationale.correct: IV amiodarone can cause hypotension, bradycardia and phlebitis; monitor blood pressure and rhythm closely.

perOption.a: This shows the drug is working.
perOption.b: IV amiodarone can cause hypotension and bradycardia; this needs action.
perOption.d: Monitor the site, but hypotension is more urgent.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

segments.text: cyanotic around the lips with an SpO2 of 84%

rationale.correct: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, hypoxemia and missed antiseizure doses need immediate action.

perOption.s2: A seizure longer than 5 minutes is status epilepticus.
perOption.s4: Hypoxemia needs airway support and oxygen.
perOption.s8: Missed antiseizure doses are a likely trigger.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize status epilepticus.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client is in {{b1}}, most likely triggered by {{b2}}.

options.text: status epilepticus
a simple febrile seizure
a syncopal episode
missed levetiracetam doses and an acute infection
low blood sugar
too much oxygen

rationale.correct: Missed antiseizure medication and acute illness are common triggers of status epilepticus.

perOption.b1:a: Seizure activity longer than 5 minutes is status epilepticus.
perOption.b1:b: Febrile seizures occur in young children and are brief.
perOption.b1:c: Syncope is brief and does not cause prolonged convulsions.
perOption.b2:a: Missed doses and illness lower the seizure threshold.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

rationale.correct: In status epilepticus, check glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, drug levels and toxicology to find reversible causes.

perOption.r2:c1: Low drug levels are a likely cause.
perOption.r3:c1: Not related to the acute seizure.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize tests in status epilepticus.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse take right away? Select all that apply.

options.text: Turn the client onto the side and suction the mouth as needed
Give oxygen by non-rebreather mask
Note the time the seizure started and its features
Place a bite block between the teeth
Hold the arms and legs down to stop the movements

rationale.correct: During status epilepticus: protect the airway, give oxygen, prevent injury, time the seizure and prepare emergency drugs.

perOption.d: Nothing goes in the mouth during a seizure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Take immediate action in status epilepticus.

questions.stem: The client has an IV in place. Which medication should the nurse expect to give first to stop the seizure?

options.text: IV fosphenytoin as the first drug
IV lorazepam, given right away as the first drug
Oral levetiracetam through a nasogastric tube
IV haloperidol to calm the jerking movements quickly

rationale.correct: Status epilepticus: benzodiazepine first (IV lorazepam, or IM midazolam), then a second-line drug such as fosphenytoin, levetiracetam or valproate.

perOption.a: Fosphenytoin is a second-line drug after a benzodiazepine.
perOption.b: A benzodiazepine such as IV lorazepam is the first-line treatment for status epilepticus.
perOption.c: Oral drugs act too slowly and are unsafe during a seizure.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The bleeding is most likely caused by {{b1}}, and the client's risk factors include {{b2}}.

options.text: uterine atony
a cervical laceration
a clotting disorder
a large baby, long labor, oxytocin and magnesium
the client's asthma
a short labor with no medications

rationale.correct: Risk factors for uterine atony include a large baby, long or induced labor, oxytocin use, magnesium and overdistention.

perOption.b1:a: A soft, boggy uterus is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage.
perOption.b1:b: Lacerations bleed with a firm uterus.
perOption.b1:c: A boggy uterus points to atony.
perOption.b2:a: These overstretch or tire the uterus or relax its muscle.
perOption.b2:b: Asthma is not a risk factor for atony.
perOption.b2:c: This does not match the history.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze the cause of postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Increase the oxytocin infusion as prescribed
Give methylergonovine, the fastest available drug
Give carboprost as the first drug
Wait for the next pad check in 15 minutes

parameters.text: Fundal tone and amount of bleeding
Deep tendon reflexes at the knees
Weight of the infant at the next feeding
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: PPH from atony: fundal massage, oxytocin, other uterotonics chosen around contraindications, IV fluids and blood, with monitoring of tone, blood loss and vital signs.

perOption.c1: A boggy uterus with heavy bleeding and signs of hypovolemia.
perOption.c2: This causes sudden collapse and breathing failure.
perOption.c3: The placenta has been delivered; atony is the more likely cause.
perOption.c4: Rupture usually happens during labor with severe pain.
perOption.a3: It is contraindicated with the client's preeclampsia history.
perOption.p1: Show whether the uterus is contracting and bleeding is slowing.
perOption.p3: Magnesium has been stopped; reflexes are not the main guide now.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care for postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse anticipate while the team treats the hemorrhage? Select all that apply.

options.text: Send blood for a type and crossmatch
Draw a complete blood count and clotting studies
Weigh pads and drapes to measure blood loss
Insert a second large-bore IV catheter
Delay labs until the bleeding stops
Empty the bladder with a catheter if it is full

rationale.correct: PPH care includes type and crossmatch, CBC and clotting studies, measured blood loss, two large IVs and bladder emptying.

perOption.b: Guides replacement and checks for coagulopathy.
perOption.c: Quantitative blood loss is more accurate than estimates.
perOption.d: Allows fluids and blood to be given quickly.
perOption.f: A full bladder prevents the uterus from contracting.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges

questions.educationalObjective: Plan supportive care for postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Bleeding continues despite fundal massage and oxytocin. Which additional uterotonic is safest for this client?

options.text: Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM
Misoprostol as prescribed
Carboprost 250 mcg IM
Magnesium sulfate restarted at 2 g/hr

rationale.correct: Choose uterotonics around contraindications: avoid methylergonovine with hypertension and carboprost with asthma; misoprostol and tranexamic acid are options.

perOption.a: Contraindicated with hypertension and preeclampsia history.
perOption.b: Misoprostol can be used with asthma and hypertension.
perOption.c: Carboprost can cause bronchospasm in clients with asthma.
perOption.d: Magnesium relaxes the uterus and worsens atony.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

caseStudies.title: Status epilepticus after missed antiseizure doses

exhibits.title: Medical unit, 1400
exhibits.body: A 41-year-old client with epilepsy was admitted with pneumonia. The client has missed two doses of levetiracetam because of vomiting. At 1355 the client began a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The seizure is still going at 1402, and the client is cyanotic around the lips with drooling.

exhibits.title: Labor and delivery, 30 minutes after birth
exhibits.body: A client gave birth vaginally to a 4.3 kg (9.5 lb) infant after a 22-hour labor with oxytocin augmentation. The client has asthma and had magnesium sulfate earlier for preeclampsia, which has been stopped. The nurse finds the fundus soft and 2 cm above the umbilicus, and the pad is soaked with bright red blood and clots.
